hints: Remember that oxidation happens at the anode (negative ions or water lose electrons) and reduction happens at the cathode (positive ions or water gain electrons).

For the molten salt there is no water present, so only the ions from the electrolyte can discharge. For aqueous solutions, think about competition between the electrolyte ions and $\text{H}^{+}$ / $\text{OH}^{-}$ from water.
Recall the discharge rules: concentrated halide solutions favour halogen at the anode, and at the cathode $\text{H}_{2}$ forms unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen such as copper.
walkthrough:
Sort out what can move to each electrode**
Think of electrolysis as a sorting game. Positive ions go to the negative cathode to gain electrons, negative ions go to the positive anode to lose electrons. With inert electrodes the electrodes themselves do not react, so the products come only from the ions present.

Deal with the molten case first**
In molten $\text{PbBr}_{2}$ there is no water, only $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ and $\text{Br}^{-}$. So at the anode: $2\text{Br}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Br}_{2} + 2e^{-}$, bromine is liberated. At the cathode: $\text{Pb}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Pb}$, lead is liberated. This is the simplest case.

Apply selective discharge to concentrated $\text{NaCl(aq)}$**
Now water is present, so there is competition. At the anode $\text{Cl}^{-}$ competes with $\text{OH}^{-}$ from water. Because the brine is concentrated, $\text{Cl}^{-}$ discharges preferentially: $2\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cl}_{2} + 2e^{-}$. At the cathode $\text{Na}^{+}$ competes with $\text{H}^{+}$ from water. Sodium is very reactive, far above hydrogen, so water is reduced instead: $2\text{H}^{+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}$ (or $2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2} + 2\text{OH}^{-}$).

Apply selective discharge to $\text{Cu(NO}_{3})_{2}\text{(aq)}$**
At the anode $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ compete. Nitrate is very hard to oxidise, so $\text{OH}^{-}$ from water discharges to give oxygen: $4\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{O}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} + 4e^{-}$. At the cathode $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ competes with $\text{H}^{+}$. Copper is below hydrogen in reactivity, so $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}$ and copper metal plates out.

Final answer: $\text{PbBr}_{2}(\text{l})$: anode $\text{Br}_{2}$, cathode $\text{Pb}$
concentrated $\text{NaCl(aq)}$: anode $\text{Cl}_{2}$, cathode $\text{H}_{2}$
$\text{Cu(NO}_{3})_{2}\text{(aq)}$: anode $\text{O}_{2}$, cathode $\text{Cu}$

hints: Think about what $F$ means (charge on one mole of electrons) and what $L$ means (number of particles per mole), then link them through the charge on a single electron, $e$.
walkthrough:
Link charge per mole to charge per particle**
Picture one electron carrying a tiny charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ $\text{C}$. One mole contains $L$ electrons. So the total charge on one mole of electrons, which is exactly the Faraday constant $F$, is just $L$ lots of $e$. That gives $$F = Le$$
Final answer: $F = L \times e$, where $e$ is the charge on one electron ($1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ $\text{C}$).

hints: Start from the anode mass loss. Convert $0.350$ $\text{g}$ of copper into moles of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ formed using $n = m / M_{r}$ with $M_{r} = 63.5$.
Calculate the total charge passed using $Q = I \times t$, remembering to convert $30.0$ minutes into seconds.

Convert total charge into number of electrons using the electronic charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ $\text{C}$, then use the anode half equation $\text{Cu} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-}$ to find the number of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions formed.
Combine the two routes to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (moles from mass and number of ions from charge) using $L$ = number of ions divided by moles.
walkthrough:
Find moles of copper dissolved from the mass loss**
At the copper anode, copper atoms are oxidised: $\text{Cu} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-}$. The mass lost is copper entering solution as $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. So $$n(\text{Cu}^{2+}) = m / M_{r} = 0.350 / 63.5 = 5.51 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ Keep this number safe, it tells you how many moles of ions your counted particles correspond to.

Find total charge passed**
Charge is current times time in seconds. Convert time first: $30.0$ minutes $= 30.0 \times 60 = 1800$ $\text{s}$. Then $$Q = It = 0.600 \times 1800 = 1080 \text{ C}$$ This is the total push of electrons through the circuit.

Count electrons, then count copper ions**
Each electron carries $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ $\text{C}$, so number of electrons is $$N(e^{-}) = Q / e = 1080 / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 6.75 \times 10^{21}$$ But look at the half equation, every $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ needs $2$ electrons. So $$N(\text{Cu}^{2+}) = N(e^{-}) / 2 = 6.75 \times 10^{21} / 2 = 3.375 \times 10^{21} \text{ ions}$$

Scale up to one mole to get $L$**
You now know that $5.51 \times 10^{-3}$ $\text{mol}$ contains $3.375 \times 10^{21}$ ions. The Avogadro constant is ions per mole: $$L = N / n = 3.375 \times 10^{21} / 5.51 \times 10^{-3} = 6.12 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$ This is reassuringly close to the accepted $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ $\text{mol}^{-1}$, the small difference comes from experimental error.

Final answer: moles $\text{Cu}^{2+} = 0.350 / 63.5 = 5.51 \times 10^{-3}$ $\text{mol}$
$Q = It = 0.600 \times 30.0 \times 60 = 1080$ $\text{C}$
number of electrons $= 1080 / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 6.75 \times 10^{21}$
number of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions $= 6.75 \times 10^{21} / 2 = 3.38 \times 10^{21}$
$L = 3.38 \times 10^{21} / 5.51 \times 10^{-3} = 6.12 \times 10^{23}$ $\text{mol}^{-1}$
